papers.title: A Practical Proprioceptive Data Collection Utility for the Unitree GO1
papers.abstract: The Unitree Go1 is a widely used platform for legged robotics research, yet collecting proprioceptive data from it is unnecessarily difficult: the Unitree SDK is sparsely documented, and ROS1 (Robot Operating System), the Go1's native middleware, is fully deprecated. We present an open-source graphical utility that enables researchers to reliably record proprioceptive data from the Go1, including joint states, IMU (Inertial Measurement Unit) readings, foot force sensor data, and gyroscope measurements, without requiring ROS expertise. The tool provides a simple GUI (Graphical User Interface) for starting, stopping, and labeling recordings in real time. The contribution of this paper is the collection utility. We characterize the acquisition quality of 51 recordings collected with it, including the achieved sampling rate and repeated samples. As a secondary, deliberately modest check that the data is useful, we train a terrain classifier on it. The results are weak: a Temporal Convolutional Network reaches about 38% accuracy on held-out recordings across ten terrain classes (10% would be chance), and a window-level split that ignores recording boundaries inflates the same measurement to about 99%. We report this as a demonstration that the logged signals carry terrain information, not as a competitive classifier. The utility is designed to lower the barrier to collecting Go1 proprioceptive data without ROS.

papers.title: An Open-Source ROS 2 Framework for Shared Control in Surgical Teleoperation: Integrating the Haply Inverse3 with the da Vinci Research Kit
papers.abstract: Surgical teleoperation deprives surgeons of touch, forcing visual inference of tissue forces; the commercial platforms now restoring force feedback remain closed, preventing open research on haptic shared control. This paper provides a system contribution: it presents an open-source, ROS 2-native framework that integrates the compact, three-degree-of-freedom (3-DOF) Haply Inverse3 haptic device with the da~Vinci Research Kit (dVRK). The framework includes a novel mapping strategy that combines 3-DOF translational device input with separately tracked VerseGrip orientation into 6-DOF patient-side manipulator commands. Two virtual-fixture-inspired guidance modes serve as reference implementations to evaluate the framework in a within-subjects user study on a teleoperated hot-wire benchmark task in simulation, and the architecture is further demonstrated on physical dVRK hardware. Relative to unassisted manual control, linear guidance significantly reduced both the number of wire contacts and the task completion time, whereas the progressive-stiffness guidance produced consistent but statistically non-significant trends in the same direction. Subjective ratings of workload, agency, and satisfaction showed favorable descriptive trends for the guidance modes. The results demonstrate the feasibility of haptic shared control with a compact device coupled to the dVRK and provide an openly available, reproducible platform for future research. They further suggest that simpler linear feedback may be more robust for inexperienced operators than more complex profiles.

papers.title: PUPPET: Physical-Unified Platform for Presence, Embodiment, and Teleoperation
papers.abstract: Remote access to robotics hardware does not by itself guarantee usable experimental data. A teleoperated trial can complete the task and still produce an incomplete or inconsistent record. PUPPET aims to solve this problem by presenting a cyber-physical framework that opens a physical robotics laboratory through a continuously synchronized VR replica of the robot, stranding environment, and task objects. In addition, PUPPET integrates a trial validation pipeline built into the experimental workflow. We evaluated PUPPET in a within-subject study with 30 participants, who performed the same table-to-shelf object-transfer task in person, through 2D teleoperation, and through PUPPET. VR reduced post-learning completion time by 27.7% over 2D (68.7,s vs. 95.0,s), statistically indistinguishable from in-person execution (72.1,s). It also produced more validation-ready (85.6% vs. 66.0%) and intervention-free (89.7% vs. 67.2%) trials. With PUPPET we show that modality shapes the remote task performance and the reusability of the resulting experimental record.

papers.title: A Tutorial on Complementarity-Based Contact Models for Robotics
papers.abstract: Simulating rigid-body dynamics with contact is fundamental to robotics, from motion synthesis and control to mechanism design. Many widely used simulators rely on cone complementarity formulations, whose physical assumptions and numerical solution require substantial background. While excellent surveys, monographs, and course notes exist, they mostly address computational mechanics or computer graphics or document a single simulator. To the best of our knowledge, a self-contained pedagogical treatment for robotics, bringing these formulations and their solvers together with complete derivations and a unified notation, does not yet exist. This tutorial addresses this gap by connecting rigid-body dynamics, conic optimization, and frictional contact. In particular, we explain how complementarity conditions encode non-penetration and frictional dissipation, determining separation, sticking, and sliding without prescribed contact modes. We distinguish equivalent transcriptions from convex relaxations, showing how the latter can introduce artifacts such as lift-off and creep. We examine the existence and uniqueness of motion and contact forces, including the solver's role in selecting among multiple solutions. We then compare first-order and Newton-based methods, explain regularization and proximal strategies, and discuss trade-offs between computational cost, robustness, and physical fidelity. Connections to widely used simulators, optimal control, and differentiable simulation help readers interpret simulation results, choose suitable formulations and solvers, and develop their own contact dynamics routines.

papers.title: PhyDEX: A Benchmark for Physical Reasoning in Vision-Language-Action Models via Dynamic Extrinsic Dexterity
papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have advanced rapidly in language-conditioned robotic manipulation, yet existing benchmarks mainly evaluate gripper--object contact and largely ignore how objects interact with the environment through gravity, friction, inertia, and mass distribution. As a result, it remains unclear whether current policies truly understand physics or merely interpolate from their training data. We address this gap through the lens of dynamic extrinsic dexterity and introduce PhyDEX, a throwing benchmark in which a robot must infer an object's mass, center of mass, and friction to send it to a destination beyond its kinematic workspace. PhyDEX contains 35K trajectories (143 hours) across nine tasks and 100 scenes, covering uniform, irregular, and dynamic-mass objects with static, multiple, and moving destinations. All data are generated by a scalable, fully automatic pipeline that combines grasp generation, motion planning, and closed-loop throw optimization under randomized physical properties. We evaluate three representative VLAs, GR00T N1.7, DynamicVLA, and ForceVLA, and find that all achieve success rates below 3\%. Our analysis reveals two key bottlenecks: limited robustness of pretrained models, which causes most failures before the throw, and physical blindness, as providing ground-truth physical properties roughly doubles success. Experiments on a humanoid robot and in the real world show the same failure patterns. We hope PhyDEX will drive the development of physically grounded robot policies.

papers.title: UniVEP: Unifying Velocity and Endpoint Prediction for Robot Manipulation
papers.abstract: Flow-matching robot policies usually use one prediction target throughout action generation, even though recovering actions from noise and polishing nearly clean actions bring different challenges. We systematically compare velocity prediction (V), endpoint prediction (X), and velocity-weighted endpoint prediction (X--V) across multiple robot policies, benchmarks, and inference budgets. On StarVLA and LiLa-WAM, X--V works best for few-step generation, while V gains more from iterative refinement. We further uncover their complementary strengths across noise levels: clean actions have concentrated covariance spectra, endpoint predictions stay more stable under high noise, and velocity predictions offer more accurate corrections near clean actions. Inspired by these findings, we introduce UniVEP, which learns both prediction targets together with consistency supervision and switches from endpoint recovery to velocity refinement as noise drops. Each step only needs one network run, and joint training also boosts single-step endpoint generation. Tests on simulated and real-world manipulation show better success rates and efficiency. On RoboTwin, UniVEP hits 61.36% success with one StarVLA run, beating the best single-target baseline at sixteen runs (59.96%). With LiLa-WAM, two runs outperform the best sixteen-step single-target baseline and cut inference latency by 77.1%.

papers.title: Awaken-HI: Scaling Humanoid Intelligence with Whole-Body Human Experience
papers.abstract: A central goal of humanoid robotics is for robots to perform the everyday work people do in homes and workplaces. Existing egocentric video datasets cover many of these activities but provide little synchronized whole-body motion data for learning loco-manipulation at scale. We build Awaken-Human, which pairs approximately 50,000 hours of egocentric stereo video with synchronized whole-body human motion and covers more than 100 skills. Building on this, we also introduce Awaken-HI (Humanoid Intelligence), a vision-language-action model for humanoid loco-manipulation that jointly predicts original human motion and retargeted robot actions through a shared action expert. We show that loco-manipulation skills transfer more effectively from people to humanoids when human trajectories directly supervise the shared action expert. Increasing human pretraining data reduces held-out robot action prediction error according to an empirical scaling law and raises the mean success rate on downstream real-robot tasks. After full-corpus pretraining and T800 adaptation, Awaken-HI achieves a mean success rate of 93.75% across eight individual tasks and outperforms GR00T N1.7 and $π_{0.5}$ in both individual and long-horizon evaluations. The same policy generalizes to objects unseen during robot post-training and to new pairings of familiar objects and destinations.

papers.title: JARVIS: An Agent That Designs, Builds, and Tests Circuit Boards on Its Own
papers.abstract: Power electronics is central to the energy transition, but developing new hardware still relies on human-led design, fabrication, testing, and iteration. We present JARVIS, an embodied AI agent that autonomously closes this loop for circuit boards. JARVIS maintains machine-specific capabilities and constraints, scans its workspace using a robot-mounted 3D scanner, and constructs an executable digital twin in which it rehearses robot motions, fabrication steps, and circuit behavior before consuming materials. A single text instruction initiates the physical experiment. Using unmodified desktop equipment, the agent coordinates a robot arm, a PCB printer that deposits conductive silver ink and solder paste, and a pick-and-place machine. It verifies progress using cameras and sensors, then tests the fabricated circuit with an OPAL-RT real-time simulator and an oscilloscope. Based on the measurements, JARVIS diagnoses deviations from the design and generates a revised design in KiCad for subsequent rehearsal. In a demonstration involving a 60 Hz notch filter for grid-connected converter sensing, JARVIS completed a first-run experiment in 2 h 39 min without human intervention, achieving 50.6 dB attenuation at 60 Hz. Its digital-twin rehearsal identified five issues before fabrication, including a test criterion that would have incorrectly rejected a functioning board. During execution, the agent also resolved encountered faults autonomously. These results demonstrate an integrated agent-driven workflow for physical design, fabrication, measurement, and iterative improvement of power-electronic circuitry. To our knowledge, JARVIS is the first system in power electronics in which an agent closes the physical design-build-test-learn loop for circuit boards.

papers.title: Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion
papers.abstract: Multi-Robot Motion Planning (MRMP) requires trajectories that avoid environmental obstacles and collisions between robots in a shared workspace. Diffusion-based planners often address obstacle avoidance through sampling-time guidance, while some conditioned approaches aggregate map geometry into a global representation. We present Spatially Conditioned Trajectory Diffusion (SCTD), a map-conditioned trajectory generator for multi-robot planning. SCTD retains multiple position-aware occupancy tokens accessed through cross-attention throughout a temporal U-Net, with hard endpoint inpainting enforcing start and goal states. One model trained on single-robot demonstrations across procedural environments generates obstacle-aware trajectories without sampling-time obstacle-cost guidance. High-level Conflict-Based Search (CBS) coordinates these trajectories through constrained replanning, retaining inter-agent guidance during sampling and reusing the model across workspace layouts and team sizes. Experiments assess single-robot success and trajectory quality, generalization to unfamiliar layouts with added obstacles, and coordinated multi-robot planning. On 15,000 held-out tasks, SCTD achieves higher success than the evaluated guided diffusion baseline, with the largest gains on hard-detour tasks, while trajectory-quality comparisons show smoother trajectories. Conditioning ablations show higher success with spatial tokens than with a global map embedding, and map-replacement tests demonstrate dependence on the supplied geometry. The resulting multi-robot system achieves higher team success than the compared diffusion baselines, with experiments covering teams of up to 15 robots.

papers.title: Towards consensus on practical probabilistic evaluation metrics for clinical decision making in radiotherapy
papers.abstract: Introduction: The main aim of this paper is to identify clinically feasible probabilistic evaluation approaches for radiotherapy and to assess whether they can support clinical decision making better than current robustness evaluation approaches. To this end, we calibrate probabilistic clinical goals and identify evaluation metrics with a team of medical physics experts and apply these to three patient cohorts. Methods: Sixty intensity-modulated proton therapy plans from three Dutch proton centers were included: 20 neuro-oncological, 20 head-and-neck, and 20 breast cancer cases. Probabilistic evaluation was performed using polynomial chaos expansion with 10,000 simulated fractionated treatments per case. Volumetric and dosimetric CTV goals were calibrated at a 90% probability level. Selected probabilistic evaluation metrics were applied to representative patient cases and eight radiation oncologists participated in semi-structured interviews addressing preferred metrics and probability levels. Results: The calibrated volumetric goals were V0.95Dpres = 99.95%, 99.80% and 99.54% at a 90% probability level for the neuro-oncological, head-and-neck, and breast cohorts, respectively. The dosimetric goals were D98%,CTV = 0.973Dpres, 0.968Dpres and 0.967Dpres at a 90% probability level. All radiation oncologists considered the probabilistic evaluation metrics suitable for clinical decision making, and most regarded them as an improvement over the currently used VWmin/max approach. Preferences for individual metrics and probability levels varied among radiation oncologists, centers and treatment sites. Conclusion: Probabilistic evaluation metrics are expected to be clinically usable and an improvement over current methods by the interviewed radiation oncologists. Further consensus and clinical validation are needed before widespread clinical implementation.

papers.title: Colloquium: Isotopes for medicine and fundamental physics
papers.abstract: Isotopes, variants of elements distinguished by their neutron number, have important applications for medicine and fundamental science. This review explores the historical challenges and new technologies for enriching and detecting isotopes. We motivate the work by challenges posed by three of history's greatest scientists: James Clerk Maxwell's thought experiment on thermodynamics, Ernest Rutherford's practical dilemma in radiochemistry, and Albert Einstein's questions about the probabilistic nature of quantum mechanics. The journey to meet these challenges has catalyzed the development of innovative techniques for isotope separation. These advancements can mitigate the worldwide crisis in the supply of enriched isotopes. We then explore the expected impact of these new technologies on medicine, which include radioisotopes for cancer therapy and stable isotopes as tracers for metabolism. We explain the importance of developing scalable techniques for isotope detection and how it can help with early detection of certain diseases. Finally, we turn to basic science, outlining proposed new tests of quantum mechanics that utilize radioactive atomic clocks to probe the fundamental nature of determinism and distinguishability of atoms.

papers.title: Physics-Informed Deep Learning for Shear Wave Speed Estimation in MR Elastography
papers.abstract: Objective: Magnetic Resonance Elastography (MRE) is a non-invasive imaging technique for mapping biomechanical properties of in vivo tissue, including shear wave speed (SWS), but involves intrinsically slow data acquisition and an ill-posed wave inversion. Instead of relying on handcrafted image priors, we propose a data-driven approach jointly combining image reconstruction and MRE inversion for robust SWS estimation from undersampled k-space data. Methods: Our physics-informed reconstruction framework comprises two blocks: a model-based neural network (NN)-regularized reconstruction module and a phase-gradient inversion (k-MDEV) calculating SWS from the reconstructed images. Concatenating both blocks yields an end-to-end trainable method to estimate SWS directly from measured k-space data. We evaluated the method on retrospectively highly undersampled brain MRE data and compared it to a total variation (TV) minimization-based approach. We assessed the impact of end-to-end training (qualitative images and SWS maps as targets) versus pre-training (qualitative images as targets) and applied the method also to in vivo data. Results: Our approach significantly reduces NRMSE by 30% compared to TV. End-to-end training improves SWS estimation over separate image reconstruction and SWS calculation. Conclusion: Accurate SWS quantification is possible at acceleration factors up to 19. Our method significantly outperforms TV, highlighting the need for data-driven regularization in this challenging MR problem. Further, our approach successfully generalizes to in vivo data. Significance: We present the first end-to-end trainable MRE reconstruction method for estimating SWS maps directly from k-space. NN-based reconstruction can enable rapid stiffness mapping for dynamic studies, functional imaging, and real-time clinical feedback.

papers.title: Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM) to evaluate the primary stability of the pedicle screw: A proof of concept
papers.abstract: The long-term success of spinal instrumentation depends on the initial stability of pedicle screws (PS), yet current intraoperative assessments rely on surgeon subjectivity. This study introduces a quantitative, non-invasive approach-the Impact-Based Analysis Method (IBAM)-to support intraoperative decision-making. The IBAM measures screw stability using low-amplitude impacts delivered with an instrumented hammer on the surgical screwdriver after screw insertion. An IBAM indicator, defined as the average time difference between the two earliest local maxima in the force signal, was analyzed under varying stability conditions in artificial bone samples. Experimental factors included bone density ($ρ$), insertion depth ( D ), and pilot hole diameter ( $Φ$ ). The IBAM indicator was compared with the PS pull-out force for each configuration. Although the main effects showed opposite trends for the pull-out force and the IBAM indicator, their relative magnitudes were similar ( $ρ$ $\sim$35%, D $\sim$25%, $Φ$ $\sim$15%). The relationship between the pull-out force and the IBAM indicator followed a power-law model (adjusted R 2 =___0.85) with a negative exponent. As screw stability increased, the pull-out force rose while the IBAM indicator decreased, demonstrating complementary sensitivity to bone-implant interface changes. While results are promising, the simplified experimental design limited the ability to fully capture bone-implant interaction complexity. Future studies should aim to validate IBAM in vivo to confirm its clinical applicability..

papers.title: Transition Dynamics Matter: Hidden Markov Scoring of Epileptogenic Channels in SEEG
papers.abstract: Stereo-electroencephalography (SEEG) represents the most effective technique for the detection of the Epileptogenic Zone (EZ) in drug-resistant epilepsy. This procedure produces a multi-dimensional signal with hundreds of components, named channels, each associated with a different brain location. In this work, we propose a joint Hidden Markov Model (HMM), in which each SEEG channel is described by a latent Markov chain, with states shared across the network and channel-specific transition probabilities. Accordingly, we develop a detection algorithm that identifies the channels belonging to the EZ by quantifying, through the Kullback-Leibler divergence, the difference between their transition probabilities in the inter-ictal period and at seizure onset. We evaluate our framework in SEEG recordings from 30 patients with drug-resistant epilepsy and compare it with a benchmark that operates in the same observation space but does not consider a latent-state structure. Compared against medically validated EZ definitions, our study shows that modeling channel-specific temporal transitions can improve EZ localization and offer a data-driven framework to investigate the latent dynamics underlying seizures.

papers.title: From real to synthetic: PSG-GAN learns sleep apnea signal dynamics for AI training
papers.abstract: Synthetic polysomnography (PSG) data has great potential in healthcare applications, for example in substituting real data that is sensitive and challenging to collect. Previous research on synthetic PSG data has been largely focused on short segments of individual signals, overlooking the inter-signal dynamics related to sleep disorders. In this study, we developed a generative adversarial network (PSG-GAN) for co-synthesizing longer segments of multiple PSG signals with diverse and complex characteristics typical of obstructive sleep apnea (OSA). The synthetic signals appeared realistic, and the electroencephalography and electrooculography band powers were similarly distributed across sleep stages. Moreover, the PSG-GAN learned to mirror signal interactions such as changes in photoplethysmography-based heart rate during and after breathing obstructions. An automatic scoring model trained solely with automatically scored synthetic signals reached good performance on sleep staging (\k{appa}=0.71 and 0.63) and respiratory event segmentation (\k{appa}=0.57 and 0.60), on two test sets consisting of healthy volunteers and OSA patients, respectively. This demonstrates the potential of synthetic data in supporting algorithm development for sleep diagnostics. The source code is available at https://github.com/rikuhuttunen/psg-gan.

papers.title: Unmyelinated axons alter the biological interpretation of MRI biomarkers of demyelination
papers.abstract: Quantitative MRI methods are widely used to probe white matter microstructure; yet diffusion- and relaxation-based metrics are often interpreted primarily in terms of myelinated axons, implicitly assuming a negligible contribution from unmyelinated axons. Here, combining diffusion MRI (dMRI), relaxation-based MRI, and electron microscopy (EM) in the cuprizone mouse model of demyelination and recovery, we examine how unmyelinated axons shape MRI-derived microstructural indices, including axonal water fraction and $g$-ratio. To enable quantitative cellular-level comparisons, we developed automated tools for instance-level EM segmentation of white matter, allowing morphological analysis of myelinated and unmyelinated axonal populations. We find that, in the mouse model, diffusion-derived estimates of axonal water fraction reflect contributions from both axonal populations at sufficiently short diffusion times; accounting for unmyelinated axons removes an apparent bias and reveals that this metric corresponds to the total intra-axonal space rather than myelinated fibers alone. Similarly, MRI-derived $g$-ratio estimates correlate strongly with EM only when both axonal populations are included. We further demonstrate that within-voxel $g$-ratio heterogeneity introduces a systematic negative bias of up to $8\%$, increasing with the fraction of unmyelinated axons and variability in myelin thickness. Together, these findings change the biological interpretation of MRI biomarkers during demyelination by demonstrating that unmyelinated axons are a major determinant of MRI-derived white matter indices and that combining diffusion and relaxation contrasts enables a more accurate and interpretable quantification of demyelination. They further highlight the need for quantitative biomarkers that account for axonal heterogeneity in both health and disease.

papers.title: Investigating Thermal Boundary Conductance in Monolayer Transition Metal Dichalcogenides: A Systematic Comparison of Advanced Nanoscale Thermometry Techniques
papers.abstract: Thermal boundary conductance (TBC) plays a crucial role in heat dissipation in two-dimensional (2D) devices. However, reported values for 2D material classes such as monolayer transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) can vary by more than an order of magnitude across the literature, making it difficult to determine whether these differences come from the materials themselves or from the measurement methods used. To address this issue, this article presents a systematic, cross-technique study of the interfacial heat transport in four TMD monolayers supported on a sapphire substrate, using three of the most representative methods: Raman thermometry, scanning thermal microscopy (SThM) and frequency domain thermoreflectance (FDTR). By conducting all measurements on the same sets of samples, the influence of sample-to-sample variation is minimized allowing for a direct comparison of the three approaches. The results reveal a variation in the measured values depending on both the material and the measurement technique. By directly comparing these results we can elucidate on the origin of the differences and underpin sources of uncertainty in each of the characterisation methods. Taken together, these results provide a direct experimental benchmark for studies of 2D material interfaces and offer practical guidance for the selection and interpretation of thermal metrology.

papers.title: Emergent Orbital Hall Currents in Disordered and Amorphous Materials
papers.abstract: The role of disorder in orbital transport remains a central open question in orbitronics. Using a real-space formulation of itinerant orbital angular momentum, we investigate the real-time or- bital Hall transport in single-orbital square-lattice and graphene-based systems. We demonstrate that both structural (polycrystalline and amorphous) and electrostatic disorder can generate siz- able orbital Hall currents that are absent in their pristine counterparts. Remarkably, in amorphous graphene, these currents persist over extended timescales and across a broad energy window around charge neutrality, despite the strong localization of electronic states. Consistent with recent exper- imental evidence, our findings establish amorphous quantum materials as promising platforms for disorder-engineered orbitronic functionality.

papers.title: Circuit model for gate-induced excitation of quantum Hall edges tuned by DC gate bias
papers.abstract: Edge excitations, which propagate along the edge of a quantum Hall system, are of great interest in the study of low-dimensional electron systems and mesoscopic transport phenomena. In this study, we investigate the relationship between the input voltage and the excitation waveform for gate-induced excitations. By varying the offset voltage applied to the gate, we observe that the excitation waveform changes from a first-derivative-like response to a response proportional to the input waveform in the time domain. In the frequency domain, we observe that the frequency dependence of the gate excitation changes significantly as the offset voltage crosses the pinch-off voltage. We show that these changes can be described by a single equivalent circuit model with different effective gate-2DEG capacitances on either side of the pinch-off voltage. In addition, we confirm that the effective capacitance obtained from the fitting of the model with the experimental data is consistent with the capacitance calculated from the device structure.

papers.title: Topology-Enabled Self-Verification of Quantum Hall Resistance Standards
papers.abstract: The scaling of multi-element quantized Hall array resistance standards necessitates rigorous validation that internal quantization has not broken down without relying on the verification of dissipationless edge state transport. One proposed solution is to use a Symmetric Precision Quantization Reliability criterion, a mathematical framework that statistically assures such validation strictly through outer terminal measurements of Cn-symmetric designs. This criterion essentially bounds the likelihood of hidden localized defects arising from quantum Hall breakdown and has potential uses in quantum computing and semiconductor testing but is presented in the context of its application toward quantum electrical standards.

papers.title: Field-free deterministic spin-orbit torque magnetization switching using monolayer WTe2
papers.abstract: An important step towards the practical implementation of spin-orbit torque magnetic memory is the field-free switching of the magnetization vector. In this work, we investigate spin-orbit torque-driven magnetization dynamics and switching devices comprising monolayer $\mathrm{WTe}_2$ as the spin-source material. We perform a comparative analysis of the two phases of $\mathrm{WTe}_2$, namely the $1\mathrm{T}_d$ and $1\mathrm{T}'$ with the necessary symmetries for field-free deterministic magnetization switching. We demonstrate switching in both systems and analyse the dependence of the switching dynamics on the applied bias voltage, ribbon orientation and width of the magnetic layer. Modelling the ferromagnet as an exchange-coupled macrospin within a non-equilibrium Green's function framework, we find that the $x$-ribbon geometry of the $1\mathrm{T}_d$ $\mathrm{WTe}_2$ phase generates a significantly larger current-induced spin polarization than the $1\mathrm{T}'$ phase, resulting in a larger damping-like torque on the adjacent magnetic layer and faster switching. The switching time of $1\mathrm{T}'$ devices varies strongly and non-monotonically with the width of the magnetic layer. In $1\mathrm{T}_d$ devices, it remains nearly constant over a broad range of widths, consistent with an edge-dominated torque. These results identify $x$-ribbon $1\mathrm{T}_d$-$\mathrm{WTe}_2$ as a promising spin source for field-free SOT-MRAM.

papers.title: Sliding-ferroelectric control of dipolar and quadrupolar excitons in R-stacked WSe$_2$
papers.abstract: A fundamental property of interlayer excitons is their dipolar character, enabling electrical tunability, enhanced exciton-exciton interactions and extended lifetime. It is important for studying collective phenomena and realizing novel optoelectronic devices. However, in homo- or heterostructures based on two-dimensional semiconductors, the magnitude and orientation of the dipole moment are commonly locked due to spatially confined charges and nature of the band transition. Here, we use gate-dependent photoluminescence of few-layer R-WSe2 to harness sliding ferroelectricity for controlling the exciton dipole configuration of emerging layer-hybridised excitons. The sliding-ferroelectric control enables a pronounced on/off switching of the diffusive transport of hybrid dipolar excitons, while further facilitating gradual and abrupt dipole reconfigurations with emerging quadrupolar excitons. Our optical probe reveals intermediate states of vertically aligned interfacial polarisation with magnitudes that confirm cumulative polarisation in multilayers. Overall, our work presents sliding ferroelectricity as a powerful tool to tune interlayer coupling and layer hybridisation. These results represent a step toward ferroelectric-controlled exciton interconnects and novel multi-bit optical memories.

papers.title: Fractional Charge at Dislocations from Band-Inversion Cancellation
papers.abstract: Band inversions with opposite Chern numbers cancel in the Hall response and yield counterpropagating boundary modes that can gap out. However, a bulk probe of the topology that survives such a cancellation is lacking. We here show that dislocations in inversion-symmetric two-band crystals with cancelling band inversions bind a half-integer charge, which reveals the quantized bulk polarization of the bond-centered obstructed atomic limit realized by such crystals. To demonstrate this, we continuously deform a broad class of two-band lattice models into decoupled chains, without closing the bulk gap or breaking the inversion symmetry, where the dislocation charge follows from a count of occupied bonds. Notably, the fractional part of this charge is insensitive to local perturbations of the dislocation core, and it therefore persists after the in-gap core state is removed, as we show analytically in the chain limit and numerically away from it. In the Weyl-semimetal counterpart, the response to a magnetic flux separates this crystalline charge from the charge set by the Chern number of each momentum slice. We propose that a half-integer core charge that persists after the in-gap peak disappears from the local spectrum can be detected in artificial electronic and optical lattices, with metamaterials providing complementary access to the core modes.

papers.title: Zero-Temperature Energetics of a First-Order Surface Phase Transition from Diffraction
papers.abstract: First-order phase transitions are governed by the balance between zero-temperature energy, thermal vibrational energy, and entropy, yet these contributions are rarely accessible experimentally. Here, we establish a diffraction-based route to determine them for the prototypical Si(111)-In atomic-wire system. From the temperature-dependent Debye-Waller attenuation of reflection high-energy electron diffraction (RHEED) intensities we extract distinct Debye temperatures for the low-temperature $(8{\times}2)$ ground state and the high-temperature $(4{\times}1)$ phase. The softer vibrational spectrum of the high-temperature phase yields the entropy gain that stabilizes this phase above the critical temperature $T_\mathrm{c}$. Evaluating the thermodynamic balance between internal energy and entropy at $T_\mathrm{c} = 125\,\mathrm{K}$ yields a zero-temperature energy difference of $ΔE_0 = 138\,\mathrm{meV}/(8{\times}2)$, including the difference in vibrational zero-point energies of the two phases, thus providing direct access to hidden thermodynamic parameters of a first-order surface phase transition.

papers.title: From Seed to BLOOM: Autonomously Growing a Better Out-of-Order Core
papers.abstract: Improving microprocessor performance while meeting ASIC implementation constraints like area and frequency is a complex and labor-intensive task that requires expertise across computer architecture, hardware design, and performance analysis and profiling. While large teams in industry can afford the engineering resources to target this problem across performance modeling, RTL design, and ASIC implementations, small teams of researchers and engineers cannot take on this huge engineering burden while keeping up with the pace of advancement in processor microarchitecture. Recent advancements in large language model (LLM) agents present a promising substrate to accelerate this traditionally human-intensive process. In this work, we build and evaluate MiracleGro, an agentic AI-based system that, without human intervention, analyzes cycle-level RTL behavior and synthesis results, identifies performance bottlenecks, and translates architectural ideas into RTL implementation in a leading open-source out-of-order superscalar application core, the Berkeley Out-of-Order Machine (BOOM). Taking into account cycle-exact performance, area, and critical path, MiracleGro automatically produces improved BOOM designs that drastically increase the human-optimized BOOM's performance on substantial workload suites such as SPEC CPU2017 with full reference inputs. MiracleGro achieves an 85% IPC speedup and a frequency improvement of 27% in SkyWater 130nm, resulting in a 2.34x wall-clock time speedup on the full SPEC CPU2017 intspeed benchmarks (30 trillion instructions). This result demonstrates the enormous opportunity to harness frontier models to improve state-of-the-art RTL-driven platforms for implementation-grounded microarchitecture research across hardware designs.

papers.title: Matching Architecture to Workload: Comparing RISC-V Parallel Accelerators for Energy-Efficient Embedded Computing
papers.abstract: Embedded computing demands high performance and energy efficiency across workloads with widely different computational characteristics. Choosing the most suitable execution model therefore requires a quantitative understanding of how each model maps to different workload classes. In this paper, we compare three execution models for energy-efficient embedded computing: scalar multicore, stream ing multicore, and vector processing. We use three open-source RISC-V accelerators as representative implementations: the PULP Cluster, the Snitch Cluster, and Spatz, respectively. Their open-source hardware and software stacks enable a controlled comparison based on implementations in the same 12 nm technology and a common benchmark suite. Our results reveal that no single execution model performs best across all workload classes. Spatz delivers the greatest benefits for regular and highly vectorizable compute-intensive applications, achieving up to 4.29x higher performance and 5.17x greater energy efficiency than the other architectures. However, its effectiveness strongly depends on the availability of data-level parallelism and regular computation and memory-access patterns, making it the most sensitive to workload characteristics. The Snitch Cluster performs particularly well on applications with limited parallelism and streamable memory-access patterns, providing up to 5.53x higher performance and 1.45x greater energy efficiency. Conversely, the PULP Cluster is most effective on irregular and control-dominated applications, achieving improvements of up to 5.66x in performance and 2.80x in energy efficiency. Compared with Spatz, however, the greater flexibility offered by PULP and Snitch comes at a non-negligible cost in terms of both area and power.

papers.title: MicroAssert: Microarchitecture-Aware Structured Assertion Generation for CPU Verification
papers.abstract: Automatic assertion generation reduces manual verification effort, yet existing approaches struggle to capture microarchitectural behaviors and cross-region interactions in CPUs. We present MicroAssert, a microarchitecture-aware framework that identifies functional regions directly from RTL and generates local and composite assertions through structured contracts and deterministic verification primitives. Coverage-guided feedback further improves verification completeness by progressively expanding proof-relevant RTL coverage. Evaluated on five open-source RISC-V CPUs against three existing assertion generation approaches, MicroAssert achieves 100% syntax correctness and complete branch, statement, and toggle coverage, with an average proven rate of 74.82% and Proof Core coverage of 90.96%. Mutation testing further demonstrates its advantage, achieving an average error detection rate of 28.73%, 1.99 to 3.51 times higher than existing methods. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of microarchitecture-aware assertion generation.

papers.title: FPGA-GEN: Target-Aware RTL Generation via HLS
papers.abstract: Successful C/C++ compilation does not guarantee correct or efficient FPGA hardware after high-level synthesis (HLS). FPGA-GEN is an agentic HLS-C generation workflow that encodes specification, readiness, selection, repair, and admission rules in explicit task contracts and bounded tool-feedback loops for candidate-level decisions. On HLS-Eval, five shared-context outputs per task yield 407/425 (95.8%) public-testbench passes. In a cumulative conversion campaign, FPGA-GEN admits 104/107 (97.2%) HLS-LeVeri designs under held-out co-simulation, Vivado synthesis/fit, and same-RTL evidence. In focused TensorCore screening, selected candidate 3 reports 73.7% fewer CSynth cycles and 14.6% fewer LUTs than generated/composed C0, with 26.7% more DSPs, and passes development CoSim.

papers.title: FoldSim: Scaling Cycle-Exact RTL Simulation with Hierarchical Folding and Static Scheduling
papers.abstract: RTL simulation is essential for hardware design and verification, yet its execution time grows rapidly with design scale and complexity. CPU- and GPU-based simulators exploit parallelism to accelerate RTL evaluation, but achieving high simulation throughput for large designs remains challenging. FPGA-based simulators offer higher throughput by mapping RTL computations directly onto hardware, but their scalability is constrained by FPGA resource capacity. We present FoldSim, an automated framework that enables cycle-exact simulation of large RTL designs on a single FPGA through hierarchical folding. FoldSim maps instances across the design hierarchy onto shared logic while maintaining their independent state. Given foldable module classes, its compiler constructs a static schedule that coordinates their execution, reducing dynamic synchronization overhead and making state accesses predictable. FoldSim backs state that exceeds on-chip capacity with external memory and brings it to the shared circuits as needed. A configurable DRAM model separates target-memory timing from host delays. The compiler explores replica allocations and state placement to balance resource savings against simulation time. On one AMD Alveo V80, FoldSim runs an 8-SM GPU and a 1,024-node Rocket datacenter with 4,096 processor cores. The unfolded implementations require approximately 16x and 200x as many LUTs as FoldSim's, respectively. The datacenter keeps about 1.9 GB of state in HBM, while a 4-SM GPU completes a 1024x1024 GEMM in 4.24 seconds, versus 26 hours in software RTL simulation.

papers.title: Native FPGA Hard-Block Implementation from High-Level Synthesis
papers.abstract: High-level synthesis (HLS) maps computations to FPGA hard blocks, yet often leaves their arithmetic modes, internal registers, and cascade links idle and recreates them in the fabric, costing area and timing. We present a C++ template library that reaches native hard-block implementations without modifying the HLS compiler. Templates fix source patterns, and an automatic flow picks scheduling settings and verified RTL patches. On AMD Versal, our matrix multiplication uses 2.4--4.5x fewer lookup tables (LUTs) than AutoSA systolic arrays at equal or higher estimated throughput. Our INT8 matrix--vector units reach the three multiply--accumulates per DSP of hand-written FINN RTL, versus at most 1.29 for HLS libraries. In hls4ml, Allo, and Stream-HLS, the templates cut LUTs by up to 2.7x and DSPs by up to 2x.

papers.title: Meta-RTL: Evolving Agent Harnesses for RTL Optimization
papers.abstract: Large language models enable agents to optimize RTL using EDA feedback, yet their executable search procedures remain largely hand- engineered. We present Meta-RTL, an EDA-grounded framework that evolves RTL optimization harnesses from a minimal loop while keeping the optimization model, EDA flow, and per-design budgets fixed. Compared with Dr. RTL, Meta-RTL* reduces aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 7.8%/11.0% across 20 development designs, with area reductions on 70% of them. Without further evolution, Meta-RTL* transfers to 10 unseen IC-RTL designs, reducing aggregate WNS/TNS violations by 20.5%/14.0% and total synthesized area by 12.6%. We further characterize three search mechanisms in the evolved harness and assess their contributions through ablations and a case study.

papers.title: Splice-Core: Low-Order-Bit-Splicing GEMM for Highly Energy-Efficient AI Inference Accelerators
papers.abstract: Splice-Core is a temporal-unary/binary (tub) hybrid general matrix multiplication (GEMM) unit that minimizes low-order accumulation latency, while retaining value-dependent execution for high-order activation bits. We present two novel processing element (PE) variants: (i) Splice-BP utilizing bit planes, and (ii) Splice-LUT, which selects a shared weight multiple in a single cycle. Compared to a binary systolic array, Splice-BP/Splice-LUT achieve 77.4%/76.4% geometric-mean tile energy reductions, respectively, across 26 INT4 convolutional neural network (CNN) and large language model (LLM) workloads in 45nm. Splice-LUT further increases geometric-mean tile throughput by 44.4% and reduces geometric-mean energy-delay product (EDP) by 6.13x across the 26 configurations. Across the evaluated W8A8 convolution and expert-projection workloads, Splice-BP and Splice-LUT reduce tile energy by 77.3-88.1%. Post-place-and-route INT4 yields 14%/9% smaller area for Splice-BP/Splice-LUT, compared to the systolic array.
